tip: Greek orders with take: θα πάρω το ψάρι (tha páro to psári = I'll take the fish) – παίρνω (pérno) is the standard way to say I'll have at a restaurant.
After a preposition, me is μένα, not με: για μένα (ʝa ména = for me). The short με (me) only works attached to a verb.
χύμα (chíma = loose, unbottled): κρασί χύμα is house wine from the barrel, ordered by the carafe or kilo, not the bottle.
You can answer yes by just repeating the verb: Έχει αρκετό! (échi arketó = it has plenty) – no ναι (ne = yes) needed.
Greek salad is the village salad: χωριάτικη (choriátiki = village-style) – the word σαλάτα (saláta) is understood and dropped.
First agrees like an adjective: έρχονται πρώτοι (érchonde próti = they arrive first) – masculine plural to match μεζέδες (mezédes), not a fixed adverb.
Greek keeps both negatives: κανείς δεν βιάζεται (kanís den viázete = nobody hurries, lit. nobody doesn't hurry).
και can mean also, not just and: ήρθε και ένα γλυκό (írthe ke éna glykó = a dessert came too) – before a noun like this, και adds too/even.
Treating someone has its own verb: κερνάω (kernáo) – απόψε κερνάω εγώ (apópse kernáo egó = tonight I'm treating).
στην υγειά μας (stin iʝá mas = to our health) is the standard toast – the everyday greeting γεια (ʝa) is this same word, health, shortened.
Greek drops subject pronouns, so adding one marks contrast: εμείς πήραμε σαλάτα (emís pírame saláta = WE ordered salad) – εμείς stresses whose order it was.
πόδι (pódi) covers both foot and leg: το πόδι του τραπεζιού (to pódi tu trapeziú = the table leg). Greek uses one word for the whole limb.
Clock times are plural: στις έντεκα (stis éndeka = at eleven) – the feminine plural στις agrees with the unspoken ώρες (óres = hours).
μάς έκανε τραπέζι (mas ékane trapézi = treated us to a meal, lit. made us a table) – κάνω τραπέζι (káno trapézi) is the standard invite-to-dinner idiom.
Personal names take the article: κι ο Γιώργος (ki o Yórgos = Giorgos too) – Greek says the Giorgos, dropping ο only when speaking to him directly.
